ranking.rationale: Highest degree awarded is a core, institution-level signal of academic mission and student pathways that should remain predictive across domain shifts. It captures durable differences between certificate/associate/bachelor/graduate institutions without relying on geography, race composition, or other brittle domain-identifying shortcuts.

Program mix is a strong, semantically stable driver of college outcomes across domains; the share of business degrees adds broad signal beyond highest degree level while avoiding direct geography, race, or other domain-identifier shortcuts.

Health-professions program share adds strong, semantically stable signal about institutional mission and labor-market orientation beyond degree level and business-share already selected, while avoiding brittle geography, demographics, and likely domain-identifier features.

Predominant degree awarded adds broad, institution-level academic orientation that should remain predictive across domains and complements HIGHDEG plus the two detailed program-share features without relying on geography, demographics, or likely domain-ID proxies.

Control of institution adds broad, semantically stable signal about school mission and operating model beyond degree level and program mix, while being less brittle than geography, demographics, or selectivity/price variables that often encode domain shifts or socioeconomic shortcuts.

Pell-share is a strong, broadly stable proxy for student socioeconomic composition and institutional mission that should remain predictive across domains. It adds complementary signal beyond degree mix, highest degree, and control, while being less brittle than geography, race-composition, or state identifiers and less likely to encode direct domain membership than locale/region features.

Admission rate adds strong, broadly stable signal about institutional selectivity and student sorting that complements degree level, program mix, control, and Pell share. It is more semantically tied to college quality/market position across domains than geography, race-composition, or other likely shortcut features, and is less redundant than adding another narrow CIP field.

First-generation share adds strong, broadly stable signal about student socioeconomic and academic support context beyond degree mix, control, Pell share, and admissions selectivity. It is less domain-identifying than state/region/locale and less problematic than race-composition or highly local census proxies, while remaining semantically predictive across institutional domains.

Institution-level SAT math midpoint adds strong, broadly stable signal about incoming student academic preparation and selectivity beyond admission rate/control/degree mix, while being less domain-identifying and less shortcut-prone than geography, race composition, or highly local socioeconomic variables.

Average family income adds strong, broadly stable signal about student socioeconomic resources and likely outcomes beyond selectivity, control, Pell share, first-generation status, and program mix. It is less domain-identifying than state/region/locale variables and less problematic than race-composition features, while offering complementary information not already captured by the selected set.

Instructional expenditures per student adds institution-level resource/quality signal that is broadly predictive across domains and complements selectivity, program mix, control, and student SES already chosen. It is more stable and less domain-identifying than geography, race-composition, or accreditor features, and less redundant than additional test-score variants.

Median family income adds strong, semantically stable signal about student socioeconomic resources and likely outcomes, while being less brittle than geography, race-composition, or institution-identifier features. It complements already selected low-income proxies like PCTPELL, faminc, and first_gen by capturing central tendency rather than just disadvantage share.

Share of dependent students adds broadly stable signal about student life stage and financial support structure that complements first-generation status and family-income variables without relying on race, geography, or obvious domain identifiers. It is likely more robust across distribution shifts than location, accreditor, or demographic-composition features, and less redundant than additional SAT/ACT or closely overlapping Pell-income measures.

Adds a strong, broadly stable affordability/financial-need signal that complements PCTPELL, faminc, md_faminc, first_gen, and dependent without relying on explicit geography or race. Federal loan uptake is semantically tied to students’ financing constraints and institutional price structure, which should remain predictive across domains, while avoiding the sharper domain-identifier risk of state/region/locale and the shortcut risk of demographic composition features.

Adds a broadly stable institutional quality/teaching-resource signal that complements selectivity, spending, program mix, and student SES already chosen. It is less domain-identifying and less redundancy-prone than geography, race-composition, or additional test-score variants, and should generalize better across shifts than demographic or location proxies.

Average age of entry adds strong, semantically stable signal about student composition and completion/earnings-related outcomes beyond selectivity, income, Pell, and first-generation status. It is less domain-identifying and less redundancy-prone than state/region, race-share, or additional test-score variants, and more robust than highly correlated price or demographic shortcut features.

Part-time share adds strong, semantically stable signal about student composition and institutional mission that should generalize across domains. It complements already selected age_entry, dependent, first_gen, Pell, and family-income features by capturing attendance intensity and nontraditional enrollment patterns without relying on brittle geography or race proxies.

Carnegie size/setting adds broad institutional context that is likely to remain predictive across domains and complements degree level, control, selectivity, staffing, and student composition already chosen. It captures stable differences in campus scale and mission without relying on explicit geography, race composition, or other brittle domain identifiers.

In-state tuition adds strong, semantically stable signal about institutional price tier and selectivity beyond degree mix, control, admissions rate, student SES, and spending. It is broadly predictive across domains and less brittle than geography, race-composition, accreditor, or duplicate test-score features, while being more directly informative than highly redundant alternatives like out-of-state tuition or rolled-up admission rate.

Adds major-program composition signal that is likely to generalize across domains: computer/information science share captures durable differences in institution offerings and labor-market orientation not yet covered by business/health shares. It is less domain-identifying than geography/accreditor/race-composition features and less redundant than additional admissions, income, or tuition variables already selected.

Engineering program share adds strong, semantically stable signal about institutional academic mix and labor-market orientation beyond the already selected health/business and general vocational composition features, while avoiding brittle geography, race, and explicit domain-identifier variables.

Adds a robust socioeconomic-preparation signal not yet captured by institution selectivity, family income, or Pell share. Area educational attainment should remain semantically predictive across domains, while being less brittle and less directly demographic or geographic than race-share, state, or region features.

Adds broadly stable academic-preparation signal that complements SAT math and admissions selectivity with relatively low shortcut risk. It is more semantically tied to student readiness than geography, race-composition, or institution-identifier features, and offers cleaner marginal value than redundant variants like ACT composites or ADM_RATE_ALL.

Net tuition revenue per FTE adds institution-level financial capacity and pricing structure beyond sticker tuition, selectivity, size, and student SES already chosen. It is broadly tied to resources and student outcomes in a way that should remain predictive across domains, while being less domain-identifying and less demographically shortcut-prone than state/region, race composition, or accreditor features.

Out-of-state tuition adds complementary, institution-level signal about selectivity, market position, and resources beyond in-state tuition, admissions rate, SAT, size, and spending. It is generally semantically tied to college quality/cost structure across domains, while being less brittle than geography, race-composition, accreditor, or other demographic shortcut features.

Median household income adds broad socioeconomic signal that is likely to remain predictive across domains and complements already selected student-income features with a more stable aggregate measure. It is less brittle than geography identifiers or race-composition variables and offers more new information than redundant test-score or tuition variants.

Average faculty salary adds institution-quality and resource information that is broadly predictive across domains and complements existing selectivity, spending, tuition, and program-mix features without relying on geography, race composition, or other brittle domain-identifying shortcuts.

Adds robust signal about nontraditional student composition beyond age_entry alone; this is strongly tied to persistence/earnings-related outcomes in College Scorecard and should generalize across domains better than geography, race-share, or redundant test-score features.

Adds a strong, stable affordability signal that complements PCTPELL, family-income, and loan variables while remaining more semantically tied to student financial need than geography, race-composition, or institution-identifier features; likely improves prediction through persistent socioeconomic effects without relying on brittle domain shortcuts.

Overall undergraduate enrollment adds stable signal about institutional scale and resources beyond size-set bins, tuition, and staffing already selected. It is broadly predictive across domains and less likely than geography, race-composition, or accreditor variables to act as a brittle domain identifier or demographic shortcut.

Biological/biomedical program mix adds complementary, semantically stable signal about institutional academic orientation and likely student outcomes beyond existing degree-level, control, selectivity, and current CIP features, while avoiding direct geography or demographic shortcut variables.

Average cost of attendance adds broad, semantically stable information about institutional price and resource environment that is not yet fully captured by tuition alone. It should generalize better across domains than geography, race-composition, or accreditor variables, and offers more marginal value than redundant test-score or duplicate part-time/admissions features.

Adds robust scale information via undergraduate degree-seeking enrollment, complementing CCSIZSET and UG with a less coarse measure of institutional size. Size is a stable structural predictor of resources, selectivity, and student support, and is less likely than geography, race composition, or state identifiers to encode brittle domain-specific shortcuts.

Education program share adds complementary, semantically stable signal about institutional mission and labor-market orientation beyond the already selected degree mix features, while avoiding brittle geography, race-composition, and explicit domain-identifier variables.

Adds broadly stable institutional context beyond size, control, selectivity, cost, and program mix: urbanization meaningfully affects student composition, commuting/residential patterns, labor-market access, and outcomes, while being less brittle and less direct as a domain identifier than state/region and less problematic than race-demographic composition features.

Unemployment rate adds broad socioeconomic context that should remain predictive across domains and complements existing income/Pell/first-generation features without relying on brittle geographic identifiers or sensitive demographic composition. It is likely to improve robustness more than redundant test-score, tuition, or race-share variables.

Adds a more targeted measure of part-time enrollment among degree-/certificate-seeking undergraduates, which is stably related to student persistence and outcomes beyond the broader part-time share already selected, while avoiding brittle geography, race, and institution-identifier proxies.

Share of married students adds stable signal about nontraditional student composition and life constraints beyond age, dependency, first-generation, part-time status, and family income. It is less domain-identifying than state/region/accreditor and less problematic than race-demographic composition features, while plausibly remaining predictive across shifts in institution mix.

Adds a strong, semantically stable signal about students' pre-college educational and professional environment that should generalize across domains. It complements existing income and parental-education proxies (faminc, md_faminc, median_hh_inc, pct_ba) with higher-skill neighborhood attainment, while avoiding brittle geographic identifiers like state/region and avoiding direct racial composition shortcuts.

Poverty rate adds broad socioeconomic context that is likely to remain predictive across domains and complements existing family-income and Pell measures without relying on direct geographic identifiers or sensitive demographic composition shortcuts.

Adds a student-composition signal not yet covered by the selected set: veteran share helps distinguish institutions serving older, nontraditional, workforce- and service-oriented populations beyond age, part-time status, dependency, marriage, and first-generation measures. It is plausibly tied to stable differences in completion/earnings-related outcomes across domains, while being less brittle and less domain-identifying than state/region, accreditor, race-composition, HBCU, or distance-only indicators, and less redundant than additional test-score or cost variants.

Distance-only status adds institution-delivery structure that is plausibly stable across domains and strongly relevant to student outcomes, complementing existing selectivity, cost, size, and student-composition features. It is less likely than state/region, accreditor, or race-share variables to act mainly as a domain identifier or demographic shortcut, and offers more distinct signal than redundant test-score or tuition variants.

Adds likely nonlinear signal beyond age_entry for student life stage and enrollment pattern, which is broadly predictive across domains and less brittle than geography, race-composition, accreditor, or campus-identifier features. It offers complementary stable value with low leakage risk.

Adds stable signal about academic program mix via psychology share, complementing existing CIP fields without relying on geography, race composition, or other domain-identifying shortcuts; likely useful for outcomes in College Scorecard and more robust across shifts than state/region or demographic composition features.

Net price adds institution-level affordability beyond sticker tuition, admissions selectivity, and student SES already selected. It is plausibly causally related to enrollment/completion outcomes and should transfer better across domains than geography, race-composition, accreditor, or state identifiers, while being less redundant than additional SAT/ACT variants or more niche program-share fields.

Adds a broadly meaningful academic-program signal not yet covered by the selected CIP mix: math/statistics intensity often tracks institutional rigor, selectivity, and labor-market orientation in ways that remain predictive across domains. It is more stable and less domain-identifying than state/region/accreditor or race-composition features, and less redundant than additional test-score variants.

Adds a broadly meaningful academic-program signal via physical sciences share that is likely to generalize across domains and complements already selected STEM/health/business field mix features, while avoiding brittle geography, race-composition, and institution-identifier proxies.

Adds a meaningful, relatively stable program-mix signal not yet covered: protective services/public safety offerings often track distinct institution missions and labor-market pathways beyond the already selected health/business/engineering/education fields. It is more semantically predictive across domains than geography, race-composition, accreditor, or campus-identifier features, and less redundant than additional SAT/ACT or cost variants.

Adds broadly stable academic-program composition signal not yet covered by the selected CIP fields. Social sciences share helps distinguish institution mission and student pathways in a way that should generalize across domains, while avoiding brittle geography, race-composition, and campus-identifier features. It is also less redundant than additional test-score or locale/state variables given SAT, admissions, control, and existing CIP features already selected.

Adds institution-level academic selectivity/composition signal that is usually predictive across domains and complements already selected SAT math/verbal with relatively stable, non-geographic information. It is less likely than state/region, accreditor, or race-demographic shares to act mainly as a domain identifier, and offers more marginal value than redundant ACT variants or additional narrow program-share features.

Adds a robust academic-preparedness signal that should generalize across domains and complements already selected SAT math/verbal/writing with an alternate standardized-test measure, while avoiding brittle geography, race-composition, and institution-identifier features.

Program-year tuition adds complementary, semantically stable price information for institutions not well covered by in-state/out-of-state tuition and net price fields already selected. It should improve coverage across school types without relying on brittle geographic or demographic proxies.

Adds institution-structure information that can stably affect student outcomes and operations beyond what size, control, degree level, and costs already capture. It is less likely than state/region, accreditor, or racial-composition variables to act mainly as a domain identifier or demographic shortcut, and offers more novel signal than redundant ACT/locale variants or narrow CIP fields.

ACT composite midpoint adds broadly stable academic-preparation signal beyond SAT math/verbal/writing and ACT math alone, with less OOD risk than geography, race-composition, accreditor, or campus-identifier features; it should improve coverage for institutions and applicants where ACT is more informative while remaining semantically tied to student readiness rather than domain membership.

Adds a broadly stable academic-program signal not yet covered: engineering-technology mix can materially affect outcomes beyond existing degree level, control, selectivity, cost, and currently selected CIP shares. It is more semantically tied to institution offerings than geography, race-composition, or campus-identifier variables, and offers better marginal value than redundant admissions/test-score variants or brittle demographic/location proxies.

Adds a broad, semantically meaningful program-mix signal—liberal arts/general studies share—that complements the already selected STEM/health/business field shares and should remain predictive across domains, while avoiding brittle geography, accreditation, and demographic composition shortcuts.

ACT English adds complementary academic-preparation signal beyond math/composite SAT/ACT already selected, and is more stable across domains than geography, race-composition, accreditor, or campus-identifier features. It should improve prediction with relatively low leakage and less redundancy than other remaining candidates.

Main-campus status adds institution-structure information that is plausibly stable across domains and complementary to control, size, branch count, and rolled-up admissions/tuition variables. It is less likely than state, region, accreditor, or race-composition features to act as a brittle domain identifier or demographic shortcut, while still helping distinguish branch/program campuses from primary institutions with different outcomes.

Adds a robust institution selectivity signal closely tied to student outcomes while remaining more semantically stable than geography, race-composition, accreditor, or identity-coded features; it also complements the already selected campus-level admission rate by covering multi-campus rollups.

Adds complementary net-price information for program-year institutions, covering a cost segment not captured by existing tuition and attendance features. This is institution-level and semantically tied to affordability and student outcomes, while being less domain-specific and less shortcut-prone than state, region, accreditor, or racial-composition variables.

Adds broadly stable signal about student-body composition and program mix without relying on explicit geography or race proxies. It is less domain-identifying than state/region/accreditor and less shortcut-prone than detailed racial composition variables, while still plausibly improving prediction beyond the already selected socioeconomic, selectivity, cost, and field-of-study features.

Adds broad academic-program mix information that is likely to remain predictive across domains and complements already selected CIP fields without relying on brittle geography, accreditor, or race/demographic composition variables.

Adds institution-level student-composition signal that can matter for outcomes while being less direct and less shortcut-prone than state, region, accreditor, or HBCU indicators. Among remaining options, this is a relatively stable structural feature with useful marginal information not already captured by income, age, control, size, and program-mix variables.

Adds broadly stable signal about institutional academic mix via arts/program composition, complementing already selected STEM/business/health CIP shares. It is more semantically tied to college offerings than geography, accreditor, state, or race-composition variables, which are more likely to encode domain shifts or demographic shortcuts.

Adds a still-missing academic program-composition signal with likely stable relevance across domains. Given many PCIP fields are already useful, another broad major-share feature should provide marginal value, while avoiding stronger domain-ID or demographic-shortcut candidates like state, region, accreditor, HBCU, locale, or race-composition variables.

Adds broadly stable signal about institutional academic mix via communications/journalism program share, complementing already selected STEM, health, business, education, engineering, humanities, and social-science CIP features. It is more semantically tied to college offerings and outcomes than geography, accreditor, or race-composition variables, which are more likely to encode domain shifts or demographic shortcuts.

Adds a still-unused program-mix signal with plausible stable relevance to outcomes while avoiding stronger domain-ID and demographic-shortcut candidates like state, region, accreditor, HBCU, or race-composition variables; among remaining options, this field-of-study share is likely to provide the best marginal generalizable value beyond the already selected institutional selectivity, cost, and major-composition features.

Adds a remaining academic-preparation signal that is likely to generalize across domains and complements already selected SAT/ACT midpoints. It is more stable and semantically tied to student readiness than geography, accreditor, state/region, or race-composition features, which are more likely to encode domain shifts or demographic shortcuts.

Adds distinctive, semantically meaningful program-mix signal not yet covered by selected CIP fields; construction-trades concentration is broadly predictive of student outcomes and institutional type across domains, while being less direct domain/leakage or demographic proxy than state, region, accreditor, HBCU, locale, or race-composition features.

Adds a still-meaningful academic-program signal not yet covered by the selected CIP mix: legal-professions share can capture vocational orientation, earnings structure, and completion pathways in a way that should generalize across domains. It is more semantically tied to institution offerings than geography or demographic composition, and is less likely than state/region/race-share features to act as a domain identifier or shortcut.

Adds institution program-mix signal that is plausibly stable across domains and not yet covered well by the selected CIP fields. Science-technician offerings can differentiate vocational/technical schools from broader academic institutions beyond degree level, tuition, and existing major shares. It is less likely than geography, accreditor, or race-composition variables to act mainly as a domain identifier or demographic shortcut.

Adds a still-unused academic-program composition signal that can stably affect outcomes across domains, while avoiding stronger domain-ID and demographic shortcut features like state, region, accreditor, HBCU, locale, and race-composition variables. It is less redundant than many remaining CIP fields and more semantically tied to institution mission and student pathways.

Adds a still-missing academic program-mix signal that can generalize across domains: architecture-related offerings plausibly affect earnings/repayment outcomes beyond already selected STEM/business/health fields. It is more semantically stable than geography, accreditor, HBCU, or race-composition features, which are more likely to encode domain identity or demographic shortcuts.

Adds institution program-mix signal that is likely to remain predictive across domains and is less brittle than geography, accreditor, or race-composition features. Agriculture share can capture distinctive school mission and labor-market orientation not yet covered by the already selected CIP fields, with lower risk of acting as a direct domain identifier.

Adds a remaining program-mix signal that is plausibly stable across domains and complementary to the many already-selected institutional and CIP composition features. Compared with geography, accreditor, race-share, HBCU, or region variables, it is less likely to act primarily as a domain identifier or demographic shortcut, and among the unselected options it offers the best marginal value without obvious leakage.

Adds institution program-mix signal that is plausibly stable across domains and not yet covered by the selected CIP fields. Compared with geography, accreditor, HBCU, or racial-composition variables, it is less likely to act as a domain identifier or demographic shortcut while still helping distinguish colleges with different educational focus and outcomes.

Adds remaining semantically meaningful program-mix signal beyond already selected CIP fields. Communications/technical program share can stably affect outcomes through labor-market alignment and student composition, while being less domain-identifying and less shortcut-prone than state, region, accreditor, HBCU, locale duplicates, or race/demographic composition features.

Adds institution program-mix signal that is plausibly stable across domains and not already covered by the selected CIP fields. Compared with geography, accreditor, HBCU, or racial-composition features, it is less likely to act as a domain identifier or demographic shortcut while still helping distinguish vocational/service-oriented colleges with different outcome profiles.

Adds remaining semantically meaningful program-mix signal with relatively low OOD risk. Compared with geography, accreditor, race-composition, or region/state features, this CIP share is less likely to act as a domain identifier or demographic shortcut, and it complements the already selected academic-field profile without relying on brittle location or protected-group proxies.

Adds remaining broadly meaningful program-mix signal after many stronger institutional and student-composition features are already covered. Compared with state/region/accreditor and race-share variables, it is less likely to act as a domain identifier or demographic shortcut, and it is less niche than the other unselected CIP fields.

Adds a still-missing academic program-composition signal that is plausibly stable across domains and complementary to the many already selected CIP shares. It is more semantically tied to institutional offerings than geography, race composition, or accreditation/state identifiers, which are more likely to encode domain shifts or demographic shortcuts.

Adds a remaining program-mix signal that can generalize across domains, while avoiding stronger domain-ID and demographic shortcut features like state, region, race composition, HBCU, or accreditor. Among the unselected options, this CIP field is the safest source of marginal stable predictive value.

Adds remaining semantically meaningful program-mix signal with relatively low OOD risk. Compared with geography, accreditor, race-composition, HBCU, or region/state features, this CIP share is less likely to act as a domain identifier or demographic shortcut, and it complements the many already selected academic-field composition features.

Adds a still-unused program-mix signal that can matter for outcomes while remaining more semantically stable across domains than geography, accreditor, or race-composition features. Most remaining candidates are either domain identifiers (state/region/locale), demographic shortcuts, or highly redundant variants; this degree-field share offers the best marginal robust value.

Adds remaining program-mix signal with likely stable semantics: theology/religious-vocations concentration can materially affect college outcomes beyond degree level, control, selectivity, costs, and other CIP shares. It is less domain-identifying and less shortcut-prone than state/region/accreditor or race-composition features, which are more likely to encode environment shifts or demographic proxies.

Adds remaining program-mix signal that is plausibly stable across domains and not a direct geographic or demographic shortcut. Compared with state/region/locale, race-composition, HBCU, or accreditor variables, this is less likely to encode domain identity or brittle distribution shifts, and it complements the many already-selected CIP shares by covering an omitted vocational field linked to institution mission and student outcomes.

Adds a still-unused academic program composition signal that can stably affect outcomes across domains, while avoiding stronger domain-ID and demographic shortcut features like state/region, accreditor, locale duplicates, HBCU, or racial composition variables. Among remaining options, this is the cleanest marginal institutional characteristic not already covered by selected cost, selectivity, size, and major-mix features.

Adds a remaining program-mix signal that is semantically tied to institutional offerings and likely stable across domains. Most stronger broad predictors are already selected, while state/region/accreditor and race-composition features are more likely to encode domain identity or demographic shortcuts rather than robust causal structure.

Adds broad student-origin socioeconomic context that can remain predictive across domains while being less brittle than state/region, accreditor, or institution/student racial-composition variables, which more strongly encode domain identity or demographic shortcuts and are partly redundant with already selected income and poverty features.

Institution locale adds stable structural signal about access, labor-market context, and campus setting beyond the already selected coarse locale2 indicator, while being less brittle and less likely to act as direct domain ID or demographic shortcut than state, region, accreditor, HBCU status, or racial-composition features.

Adds a modest but still semantically meaningful signal about institutional student composition without relying on coarse geographic identifiers like state/region or stronger demographic shortcuts such as large Black/White/Hispanic shares. Among remaining options, this is the least likely to act primarily as a domain label while still capturing niche mission and enrollment patterns not already covered by size, control, locale, first-generation status, and income variables.

Adds a small amount of institution-level student-composition signal beyond the already selected enrollment and socioeconomic features, while being less likely than state/region/accreditor or broader race-share variables to act as a dominant domain identifier. Most remaining candidates are either redundant race-composition proxies, duplicated older/newer variants, or strong geography/demographic shortcut features with poorer OOD stability.

Adds some remaining signal about student-body composition that can affect outcomes, while being less directly tied to protected-group shortcuts than Black/White/Hispanic share features. It is also more institution-level and semantically related to enrollment mix, offering modest marginal value beyond the already selected socioeconomic, selectivity, cost, and program features. State/region/accreditor are stronger domain identifiers, and HBCU or major race-share variables are more likely to encode brittle demographic shortcuts.

Adds modest but still potentially stable signal about student-body composition beyond already selected socioeconomic and institutional features, while being less directly tied to protected-group shortcuts and domain identifiers than state/region/accreditor variables. It is preferable to redundant race-share variants and to stronger shortcut features like HBCU or geographic identifiers.

Adds a meaningful student-composition signal not yet covered by the selected set, with likely stable association to college outcomes through mission, support structure, and peer environment. It is more semantically predictive than pure geography/domain-ID variables like state or region, and less redundant than older duplicate race-share fields.

Adds remaining student-composition signal with likely predictive value beyond academics, finances, and program mix, while being less purely geographic/domain-identifying than state or region. It is preferable to redundant race-share aliases and to stronger shortcut features like HBCU, STABBR, or region.

Adds remaining broad student-composition signal not yet covered by the selected race-share features, and is more semantically tied to institution population and outcomes than pure geography identifiers like state/region. It is preferable to redundant legacy variants and less brittle than accreditor or location codes, while avoiding the especially sensitive shortcut risk of HBCU.

Adds a broadly meaningful institutional-composition signal not yet covered: share of non-resident aliens often tracks selectivity, resources, and program mix in a way that can remain predictive across domains. It is less directly a geographic/domain identifier than state or region, and less likely to reinforce domestic racial-demographic shortcuts than the remaining race-share features, while still providing complementary information beyond admissions, SAT/ACT, tuition, and existing student-background variables.

Adds a broad student-composition signal not yet covered by the selected race-share features, and is likely more directly informative than the remaining redundant legacy race variables. It can capture persistent differences in institutional mission and student body that matter for outcomes, while being less purely geographic/domain-identifying than state or region and less brittle than accreditor.

Adds modest institution-level signal about reporting/composition not yet covered, while avoiding stronger domain-identifier features like state/region/accreditor and avoiding highly redundant or shortcut demographic composition variables already represented by selected race-share and socioeconomic features.

Most remaining candidates are redundant race-share variants or strong domain/location identifiers (state, region, accreditor) that are brittle for OOD generalization. This feature adds a small but distinct student-composition signal not already covered by the selected race-share variables, while avoiding the heavier shortcut risk of explicit geography and institution-identity proxies.

Adds a remaining enrollment-composition signal not yet covered, while being less direct as a domain identifier than state/region and less institution-specific than accreditor. It complements existing race-share features with limited marginal demographic information, whereas most other candidates are redundant duplicates or brittle geographic shortcuts.

Adds a likely informative enrollment-composition signal not yet exactly represented: the selected set includes UGDS_WHITE but not the non-Hispanic white share variant, which can matter after controlling for institution type, selectivity, program mix, costs, and socioeconomic composition. It is more semantically tied to student composition than pure geography features like state/region, and is less domain-identifier-like than accreditor or location codes.

Adds a remaining enrollment-composition signal that can matter for college outcomes while being less direct as a geographic/domain identifier than state or region. It is also less redundant than the zip-code racial composition variables and complements the already selected UGDS race-share features by capturing total undergraduate composition rather than degree-seeking-only shares.

Adds a remaining enrollment-composition signal not yet covered by the selected race-share features, while being less direct as a domain identifier than state/region/accreditor and less likely to encode brittle geographic shortcuts than census racial composition variables.

Adds institution-level undergraduate racial composition signal not yet covered by the selected UG race-share features, and is likely more directly predictive of student outcomes than broad geography or accreditor identifiers. It offers incremental value beyond existing demographics while avoiding especially brittle domain-ID features like state, region, or accrediting agency.

Adds remaining undergraduate Hispanic composition signal not yet covered by selected UG race-share features, offering some incremental institutional context. It is less directly a geographic/domain identifier than state or region and less redundant than zip-code demographic proxies, while likely more useful than accreditor or HBCU after many stronger structural and socioeconomic features are already included.

Adds a still-missing undergraduate composition signal that can matter for outcomes while being less directly tied to geographic domain labels than state/region and less redundant than broad race-share proxies already partly covered by existing enrollment and neighborhood demographics. It offers incremental institutional/student-mix information beyond UGDS_NRA and complements the selected UG subgroup features.

Adds a small but still semantically relevant enrollment-composition signal not yet covered by the selected race-share features, while avoiding stronger domain-identifier variables like state/region/accreditor and avoiding additional demographic shortcut variables from students’ home ZIPs. Its marginal value is modest but likely the most stable among the remaining options.

Adds a still-missing major enrollment-composition signal with likely predictive value beyond the already selected race-share features, while being less overtly domain-identifying than state/region/accreditor and less shortcut-prone than adding more student-zip demographic percentages or HBCU.

Adds student-origin neighborhood composition signal that can still reflect socioeconomic context and educational opportunity beyond already selected income, poverty, and race-share features at the institution level. It is less direct as a domain identifier than state/region/accreditor and less likely to encode brittle institutional identity than HBCU. Among remaining options, it offers the best marginal stable predictive value while avoiding the strongest OOD risks.

Adds institution mission/type information that can remain predictive across domains and outcomes beyond degree level, control, selectivity, and student mix. It is more semantically stable than state/region/accreditor identifiers and less redundant or shortcut-prone than additional race-composition variables already heavily represented.

Adds socioeconomic-context signal from students’ home zip codes that can remain predictive across domains, while being less direct a domain identifier than state/region/accreditor. It also complements existing income, poverty, and race-composition features without relying on institution-level demographic shares that are more shortcut-prone.

Adds socioeconomic-context signal from students’ home zip codes that can remain predictive across domains, while being less direct as a domain identifier than state/region/accreditor. It complements already selected income and poverty measures by capturing neighborhood racial composition without relying on institution-level race shares, which are more brittle and shortcut-prone.
